I have 250 hours in this game. I have achieved Completionist++. I am leading with this because I want to make clear that I do have appreciation for this game, it does a lot of things very right, and I don't necessarily think all the praise and accolades it got are unwarranted. 
 
However, it does some things very wrong which to me are fundamental to a roguelike. The biggest is that it does not manage to make losing fun. By that I don't mean that looking at the game over screen is unfun, but the process of getting there, having a subpar run you know is about to fall short, is heavily unfun. In action roguelikes this is usually more fun than steamrolling, because it forces you to play well. The basic loop of [get hit -> lock in -> survive until new item or hp drop -> stabilise -> enemies get tougher -> repeat] is fundamentally engaging and helps bridge the gap between the insane runs and meta unlocks. In balatro, this gameplay loop does not exist. The main culprit is the all-or-nothing nature of blinds. Either you reach the point threshold, or the run is over. Doesn't matter if you are 100k points off, or 1. The most obvious way this can be painful is if you misjudge your scoring, you have a glass card in your hand but think you don't need it, and end up 200 points short from a 20k blind. Tough luck, back to the main screen for you. In this case the entire process of losing was condensed into one decision. Just as frustrating is when on a random normal blind, you just fail to d

It's really hard to be negative about a game so unanimously acclaimed without sounding smug or edgy but here I go...

There's a lot to love here : the concept is awesome, the presentation is cool, everything snaps and clicks in a very satisfying way, it runs super smooth on low-end computers...

To me the issue is that Balatro fails as a roguelike deckbuilder. Every run goes as follows : in the first 3 rounds you'll pick a comp to play depending on the first jokers or tarot cards you find. Once you have picked your path, you're all in. Cross your fingers and hope to find the cards you want.

You still have agency, but there's a pretty clear better option at every intersection. Hybrid comps don't really work, mid-game transitions are super rare and usually bad choices. There is only one path and it's forward.

Roguelike deckbuilders are at their best when they keep you on the edge until the end. When every new card or random event is an opportunity to contemplate adjusting your course or even risking a 180. When they stir creative thinking, innovative comps, when they push you to unexplored paths.

Balatro is the opposite of that. Try counting the number of meaningful decisions you made in the course of a successful run. It was probably less than you thought.

don't get me wrong this is a very well crafted game for what it is. clearly a lot of love and care went into this. but to be totally honest i can't really recommend playing this. maybe i'm just burnt out on roguelikes but i felt nothing when i won my first run. it feels like this game as well as many roguelikes (i would say the same thing for nubby, slay the spire, etc)  were designed to be addictive rather than rewarding. if what you're looking for is a great way to pass time then this is fantastic. but on the whole I wouldn't describe the experience as satifying.

While I like the base game very much, the harder difficulties only serve to add tedium and RNG rather than increase the level of skill required to play the game. Fun in concept, but the challenges and higher stakes need tweaking to feel fun and rewarding rather than endlessly restarting until a run goes your way, especially for a completionist trying to experience everything the game has to offer.

Wins in higher stakes don't feel earned even when they do happen, but rather that the stars aligned for something to go the right way rather than being a result of careful play and planning. 

Above blue stake, the game gets tedious very quickly. One less discard means you can't consistently play 5-card (or even sometimes 4-card) hands like straights, flushes, full houses, 4-of-a-kind, and two pairs, negating half of the jokers in the game from being viable. Adding stickers like rental and perishable cuts down your options further, and by gold stake, it feels like you're just spinning a shop to get anything you can use for a few blinds. Win enough of those spins, you win the run. Go long enough without finding anything (in a completely RNG-based manner), and you slowly get overtaken by blind scaling and lose.

As for the game scaling itself: Some bosses are significantly stronger than others, some can end your run entirely, and the way the game is designed, it simply doesn't offer enough time to pivot from a run-killer, making running into those bosses feel particularly like a slap

The more I play this game the less I like it. It becomes evident the more you play that the difference between a good run and a bad run is rng. You can salvage a bad run in Risk of Rain, Hades, Slay the Spire or Vampire Survivors by playing really well. But if you get bad rng in Balatro there is really nothing you can do. You can play your little heart out like your name is mr John Poker and it won't matter. Pick a deck that gives more cash, have 20-40 cash after every blind and reroll the shop like crazy, if you don't get any good jokers you're screwed. Planet cards, tarots, play cards, the hands you play are completely meaningless in higher antes if you don't have good enough jokers, which is entirely dependent on rng.

Balatro is a good game, don't get me wrong - phenomenal visual and sound design with unique gameplay - but the game is designed so poorly around the challenge decks, and the issues that plague them could so easily be ameliorated, if not fixed. In general, as difficulty increases, your personal skill matters less and less, until the player-hostile RNG completely takes over and makes it feel awful to play. My first couple hours finishing the white decks were great - most everything beyond that has been a mixed to terrible experience, all due to the poorly-implemented RNG. It comes in three main parts, each of which have glaring flaws [to reiterate, at higher difficulties] - shop RNG, boss blind RNG, and deck RNG.

The most egregious part of this game is how useless the shop is for many challenge decks. It's imperative you get specific Jokers at specific times - you need score-boosting Jokers immediately to stand a chance at beating early blinds, you need money Jokers early to build up shop access, and then you need multiplicative Jokers later on to defeat the bigger blinds. Meanwhile, the game doesn't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about this and will happily give 0 score-boosting Jokers, if any Jokers at all depending on the deck. There is no other way to meaningfully scale your score, it's so foundational to the basic loop of the game, and yet I have spent actual hours in reset hell not seeing a single +mult or +chip Joker anywhere. Balatro is a ten dollar game. I had about ten dollars of fun. In that sense, I guess that makes it a good value, but I still don't think I would "recommend" it.

Balatro is, in a very pure sense, a rogue-like deck builder with a poker theme. However the gameplay takes much more heavily from deckbuilder genre staples than it does from its poker aesthetics. You try to build a deck mostly at the whims of RNG, You play progressively harder matches until your deck fizzles out. There's metaprogression that unlocks new carsd and abilities, and your ultimate goal is to get some kind of gamebreaking combination of cards that trivializes competent strategy. 

But Balatro has... a very specific problem. Balatro is a game that rewards careful planning, strategy and risk management... while a the same time having about 7 overlapping layers of RNG for every gameplay mechanic. It creates a very unpleasant feeling of knowing your fate is entirely out of your hands, while also feeling like you must micromanage what few levers you do have access to on penalty of immediate death.

To compare this to other Roguelikes...
Megabonk is a fast, silly game. It is fundamentally RNG based. There's skill in terms of game knowledge and movement optimization, and making smart build selections, but 90 percent of the game is running in circles watching the particle effects go BRRR. On a good day, I would sing my praises about this game. It is objectively good, pure fun and addictive. 
Today however, is not a good day. In light of hearing that the game studio behind Balatro (Playstack) is being sold to a notorious megacorp (VantageCo, owned by Integrated Media Company) I cannot in good faith recommend the support of this game. As of right now, the game is still in a playable state- but who knows what could happen after this acquisition, who knows how many microtransations this once quality game could be riddled with. I don't trust this company and neither does a good portion of gamers out there. That being said, I alone can't do ♥♥♥♥ but at the very least I can vocalize and protest, and maybe encourage others to look into the matter and do the same. Playstack should remain independent and not under the control of this corporate scheme.
I do no at this time recommend supporting this game. Please stop the acquisition.

Initially, I had some good fun figuring out the mechanics and climbing the difficulty ladder. The animations, music and sounds made for a very satisfying experience.

Then I reached the higher difficulty levels and the satisfaction disappeared: it didn't feel like my decisions mattered anymore. I tried all kinds of strategies, but most of runs just fell apart without warning. 

So I figured I was missing something obvious and went online to educate myself on the intricacies of high-stakes Balatro playing. Turns out it was indeed rather obvious: don't build your deck around anything more complex than High Cards or Pairs if you don't want the game to turn into a restart simulator. More complex hands like Straights or Flushes simply don't show up consistently enough.

To me, this is a cardinal sin in Roguelike Deckbuilders: higher difficulties should reward better decision making and creative adaptation, rather than strict adherence to a very limited META.

I don't regret my purchase and understand that an easy-to-pickup dopamine generator is plenty of game for some, but will give a thumbs down to voice my disappointment and somewhat mitigate the Gamer Groupthink that created the hype around this game. It's just not that deep.

Is this a good game? Strictly speaking, yes. It's a good enough game that I actually feel a little bad giving it a negative review, but I'm coming from the perspective of someone who wants to 100% every game they play, and from that side of things it's frankly pretty terrible. While most of this game's achievements are fairly inoffensive, Completionist++ was easily one of the most frustrating experiences I've had across any game I've played. With the game giving you very little way to influence what jokers you find in a run (limited mostly to filtering by rarity), compounded with some of the inherent issues of the game's higher difficulties, the task of winning on the highest difficulty with every single individual joker becomes a long, drawn-out rng check. Now, for the average player who isn't committed to getting every single solitary achievement, none of this really matters, since there's no pressure to win with specific jokers and only the higher difficulties end up exacerbating some of the punishing randomness in the game. But if you're the kind of person who won't feel satisfied unless you have absolutely everything done, I'd recommend avoiding this one (or at the very least getting ready for a long and tiring grind).

Balatro is the definition of "just fun enough." It sucks you in early as you learn the mechanics, how the jokers work, playing with different combinations. It's exciting to unlock new jokers. But then the RNG hits. And it hits hard. So much of this game is HEAVILY up to luck. You can easily waste hours endlessly resetting runs, or getting through multiple antes only to get screwed over at the last minute. Balatro can be fun, but too often that fun gives way to frustration and boredom.

Overall, Balatro is well balanced, and a consistent and fair game.
And that is what I dislike.
Every game plays exactly the same:
- Find source of flat chips
- Find source of mult chips
- Find mult
- Find mult scaling

The fun from these kinds of endless roguelikes comes from finding broken combos and interactions, and building fun decks. But this is IMPOSSIBLE in balatro for a few simple reasons:
- Every single deck except maybe 2 are hard countered by a boss, which you WILL fight sometime during a run
- The cards are all so similar in power level that there are simply only one or two broken combos, and those ONLY work with insane luck

Want to play an all five of a kind deck? Hard countered by a boss
Want to play flushes? Hard countered by a boss
Want to play face cards? Hard countered by a boss

NOTHING works in endless. NOTHING.

The game works tirelessly to ensure that all possible hand WILL eventually fail to something entirely out of your control. You may only play the most generic, boring of hands if you want to consistently succeed.

This may be fine for players with different playstyles, but for me, it entirely ruins the game and I cannot recommend it.

Its a child of poker and rogue-like. AS with most roguelike games, its cool for a couple of hours, then the novelty wears off and you realize this is just another infinte loop game. Rogue-likes have completely ruined gaming and made a mockery out of gamers...hooking people on with RNG forcing them to resort to cheap tactics, pushing the mindless grind into something absolutely masochistic and pointless - the entire genre is nothing but a big middle finger and disrespect to the time we have. Slay the spire, FTL, Balatro, Loop Hero...they're all incredibly frustrating and time wasting games that spit in your face and don't respect you or your time at all. 

IN Balatro, this mostly manifests in really crappy Jokers (power ups) and limited upgrade options most runs...some people keep resetting in the first part of the game if they dont get anything decent. 

Not a knock on the creators, who have created a brilliant stand out Rogue-like game here....but its the genre itself that has taken gaming a few steps back. Rogue-lites are generally better (Hades, Inscryption - though the latter is not strictly rogue-lite or rogue-like), though I understand the difference is night and day - but I do wish this game was more of a rogue-lite, which it could be with a few changes and tweaks, rather than rogue-like (a genre that belongs in the garbage bin, just like all the games that involve RNG-based grinding as a main aspect of the gameplay).

Likes: Addictive, easy to play, easy to come back to, and satisfying when you get the perfect build and get the high E's. (Haven't tried my hand yet at getting to naninf)

Dislikes:  Especially above white difficulty, the game seems to try and steer you in directions with jokers, tarots, and card draw (it's definitely not true random luck of the draw) which breaks the emersion for me.  As well, when you start a new game it feels like the seed is only incrementing by 1 and isn't randomized like say Minecraft or a million other games.  A lot of times I'll get the same hands and jokers when I start a new game.  What will happen is like, I'll get a string of like 2 Aces, 2 Queens, 2 8's, and 2 2's for example, then next game it will be the same with the same jokers but the card numbers will be shifted by like 1.

Overall, this game has been both awesome and pissed me off.  5/10  Be ready to get pissed and messed with above white and know what you're getting into.  I figured it'd be a game of skill to build the best deck but above white it definitely feels like the game is trying to sabotage your builds.
